laws.name: Accessory Dwelling Units and Junior ADUs
laws.summary: On a lot with (or proposed for) one single-family home, the state allows one ADU plus one junior ADU (inside the house), whatever local density says. Pasadena allows ADUs in all residential zones and in CO/CL (PMC Tables 2-2 and 2-5, §17.50.275).

citation.section: Cal. Gov. Code §§66314-66342 (recodified from §65852.2 by SB 477, effective 2025)

assumptions: Applied wherever local zoning fits at least one home: the owner may build a house plus an ADU and a junior ADU instead of what local density allows. It's an alternative path (the larger of the two counts), not added on top.
Multifamily lots can also add ADUs under state law (conversions of non-living space and up to 8 detached ADUs, SB 1211). Not modeled yet, so multifamily ADU capacity is undercounted.

laws.name: SB 9 two-unit developments and urban lot splits
laws.summary: In single-family zones, the state allows two homes on a lot by right, and a one-time split of the lot into two, each allowed two homes: four in total. Pasadena adopted this as "Two-Unit Developments" (Table 2-2 note 5) and allows no ADUs on lots created by an urban lot split.

citation.section: Cal. Gov. Code §65852.21 (two-unit developments) and §66411.7 (urban lot splits)

assumptions: Each new lot must also be at least 40% of the original; splitting a lot in half always satisfies that, so we don't check it.

SB 9 doesn't apply where the work would demolish rent-restricted housing or housing rented in the last 3 years. We don't have tenancy data, so this is not checked; capacity on rented lots is overstated.
Lots in very high fire hazard zones can still use SB 9 if they meet fire mitigation standards, so they are not excluded.
The owner-occupancy affidavit required for lot splits is a condition of approval, not a capacity limit.
Lots under 1,200 sq ft get no SB 9 units (they are almost all strips and slivers, not house lots).

laws.name: AB 2097 no parking minimums near major transit
laws.summary: Cities may not require any minimum parking for housing within ½ mile of a major transit stop (Public Resources Code §21064.3).
assumptions: Distance is measured from the nearest edge of the lot, i.e. a lot counts if any part of it is within ½ mile. Measuring from the lot's center would cover fewer lots.
Major transit stops come from SCAG's 2022 base-year inventory, which uses the AB 2553 definition (20-minute peak headways).

laws.name: SB 79 transit-oriented development (2025)
laws.summary: Near qualifying stops, cities can't hold projects of 5 or more homes below set heights, densities and floor area. Tier 1 (heavy rail): 75 ft, 120 homes per acre and FAR 3.5 within a quarter mile, then 65 ft, 100 and 3. Tier 2 (light rail, qualifying bus): 65 ft, 100 and 3, then 55 ft, 80 and 2.5. Sites within 200 ft get +20 ft, +40 homes per acre and +1 FAR. Applies from July 1, 2026. We report it apart from base capacity, in a separate row.
assumptions: Stops, tiers and half-mile zones come from SCAG's official SB 79 map. Where SCAG shows the commuter rail tier two ways, we use its SB79_TIER field.
Local delay ordinances and alternative plans, including the City of LA's phased ordinance, aren't modeled, so a lot's number may not apply yet.
Tenant history, rent-controlled demolition limits, airport and fire rules aren't checked.
Above 10 homes, a project needs 7% extremely low, 10% very low or 13% lower income homes. Average home size can't exceed 1,750 sq ft.
Floor area becomes homes using the same gross sq ft per home as the rest of the engine.

laws.name: State Density Bonus Law
laws.summary: Projects with affordable homes can exceed local density. The largest mixed-income bonus is 50%, at 24% lower income or 15% very low income homes. A 100% affordable project gets 80%, with no density limit within a half mile of a major transit stop. We report these in separate rows.
assumptions: The percentage tables come from a law firm's 2022 chart (Meyers Nave), because the state's site couldn't be read. AB 1287's extra stacked bonus for added moderate income homes isn't modeled, so numbers can run low.
The bonus needs a numeric base density of at least 5 homes, so zones limited only by floor area show no number.
Waivers can lift physical limits, so these rows ignore yards, height and parking. Each is an upper estimate.
